https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/copy-of-047128-1.png?&fit=crop&w=1600&h=900
Image via Roadside Attractions

Buddy looks like the children’s show you might have watched every morning before school, provided your parents never checked what was on TV. Its enormous orange unicorn mascot promises to be friends with everyone, even as children begin disappearing and the world around them becomes increasingly difficult to trust. The movie is funny, deeply strange, and much more interested in messing with your head than letting you settle into a familiar slasher.

Director Casper Kelly, the mind behind Too Many Cooks, takes the cheerful language of ’90s kids’ television and pushes it somewhere it was never meant to go. There’s a lot more happening inside Buddy’s show than its smiling host wants anyone to know. Audiences who came out of the movie wanting another dive into Buddy's world have something in common with one of the people who created it.

Producer Tyler Davidson wants to make a Buddy sequel. When asked in a recent interview which of his movies he would revisit with a $100 million budget, Davidson didn’t need time to think: “Very easily the answer to the first question would be doing a sequel to Buddy. There is so much more I want to explore.” A second movie has not been announced, but its producer clearly isn’t ready to leave that unicorn behind.

Your Nightmare Is…

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath
your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what
it would leave behind.
A Nightmare on Elm Street · Since 1984
Elm Street

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you
to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever
won that particular argument.

Freddy is horror's cruellest idea: a threat that lives in the one place you cannot
guard, cannot lock, and cannot avoid forever.

You are the one who is fine during the film and wide awake at two in the morning. Your
own head is where this does its damage.

These films understood exhaustion as a horror engine. The kids on Elm Street do not lose
because they are weak. They lose because they are tired.
You can lock every door in the house. You still have to sleep.
Child's Play · Chucky · Since 1988
Chucky

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the
person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Chucky works precisely because he is absurd. That is the trap: the more accurately you
describe him, the less anybody is going to believe you.

You are the one shouting at the screen because the characters are not listening. You
know that feeling from real life too.

The franchise is at its best when the adults in the room are the real obstacle, and you
have met those adults.
By the time somebody finally believes you, you will have handled most of it on your own.
Scream · Ghostface · Since 1996
Scream

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost
certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Scream is the only one of these where the killer takes the mask off and turns out to be
somebody who was at the party.

You are the person who calls the twist out loud before it lands. You watch people the
same way you watch films.

The franchise made the rules of horror part of the plot, which means the survivors are
the ones paying attention. You would be paying attention.
Everybody is a suspect, including the person who just offered to walk you home.
The Conjuring · The Warren Files · Since 2013
The Conjuring

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people
asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

The Conjuring films are domestic horror. The house, the family, the perfectly ordinary
room that quietly stops feeling ordinary.

Your instinct is to get everybody into one room. Your fear is protective rather than
personal, which is rarer than it sounds.

This is the one franchise where belief is the weapon. The people who come through it are
the ones who are not alone and refuse to be.

There’s More to ‘Buddy’ Than Its Killer Unicorn
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/buddy-2026-movie.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
Image via Sundance Film Festival

Released in theaters last month, Buddy stars Cristin Milioti, Topher Grace, Keegan-Michael Key, Michael Shannon, and Patton Oswalt. The story follows children caught inside the world of a television show whose relentlessly friendly host refuses to acknowledge that anything is wrong. It’s a premise that sounds like a joke until Buddy starts making good on the threat lurking beneath all that bright orange fur.

Davidson said the initial pitch described Buddy as a movie about a Barney-like character who goes off the rails. That’s an effective way to get someone to read the script, but it barely prepares them for the movie itself. He and producing partner Drew Sykes were drawn to how “unique and unhinged” Kelly’s idea was, and the team has been careful about how much they explain ahead of time. That restraint makes sense once the movie starts showing its hand. Davidson said Buddy has multiple layers that are better discovered while watching, and its psychological horror is what scares him most. He still considers it a slasher, despite admitting that the genre usually isn’t his thing. Buddy’s insistence that everyone is having fun becomes harder to believe as children disappear, and each new turn raises questions about the world they’re trapped in. The movie doesn’t hand over every answer just because its characters desperately need one. Those unanswered questions give Davidson plenty to explore if he gets the chance to return.

For now, Davidson’s interest is the closest thing Buddy has to a sequel announcement. The ending of the film leaves some characters' fates ambiguous, so Davidson could definitely find more horrors in this world.
Buddy is currently still playing in theaters, with no word on a streaming or digital release date yet. Stay tuned with Collider for updates.
